idiom_name: construction-time validation + copy-with updates + persistent structures with structural sharing + one version handle
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: build every value fully in a constructor or factory that validates it and copies or freezes what it receives, expose no mutator, and express each update as a pure function that returns the next version while never writing to its input. Keep the current version behind exactly one handle - a variable, an atomic pointer or a store key - and change the system only by swapping that handle, so readers always see one consistent version. For large or deeply nested data use a persistent representation that copies only the path to the change and shares the rest (cons lists, tries with path copying, copy-on-write buffers); where the language cannot express sharing, replace deep copies with a mutable transient that is frozen once. Make equality and hash follow content for anything used as a key, and treat freeze/unmodifiable/readonly markers as boundary enforcement rather than as the guarantee itself.
code_sketch:
data = build(...)                  # constructed once, validated
next = update(data, change)        # pure: returns a new version, data untouched
current.store(next)                # swap the single handle; readers keep their version
# large structures: path copying shares everything not on the update path
pitfalls: Claiming immutability while an accessor hands out mutable interior state (arrays, lists, maps, dates): the guarantee is only as deep as the shallowest accessor.
Freezing or marking read-only one level (Object.freeze, Collections.unmodifiableX, a frozen dataclass) and calling the nested data immutable.
Deep-copying the whole structure on every update where a persistent representation with structural sharing would do.
Mutating a value that is considered shared - reusing a builder after it was frozen, or writing in place to a stored snapshot - so every holder sees the change.

Retention inversion: when structural sharing keeps old nodes alive, a single long-lived root can pin a large portion of history, turning an expected GC benefit into an unbounded memory leak; measure retention and consider explicit pruning for long-running systems.

Mixing mutable and immutable collections in the same codebase: passing an immutable-collection-wrapped mutable collection (or vice versa) creates type confusion where clients believe they hold an immutable view but aliases with write access exist elsewhere.

Forgetting that getters may return mutable references: a field typed as List<T> or byte[] in an immutable class is an alias vector unless the getter returns a defensive copy or an immutable view; this is the single most common source of broken immutability guarantees in practice.

Underspecifying equality and hash for nested types: if a field used in equality or hash contains an unhashable or mutable value (e.g., a List key in a frozen map), the contract silently breaks at runtime rather than failing at construction time.

Serialization round-trip losing immutability: deserializing into an immutable type then mutating it to 'fix' incomplete deserialization undoes the guarantee; always re-validate and reconstruct through the same canonical factory as initial construction.

Wrong move: build a large persistent collection with one immutable update per item -> discarded intermediate versions create avoidable allocation and GC pressure -> instead use a scoped transient or builder and freeze once.

Wrong move: treat Erlang persistent_term as a general-purpose mutable registry -> replacement copies metadata and can trigger a system-wide garbage-collection scan -> instead reserve it for read-heavy terms that are rarely updated.

Wrong move: expose a read-only wrapper around a mutable nested graph -> aliases can still change the graph behind every snapshot -> instead recursively construct immutable or persistent child values at the boundary.
